QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Process and Governance_19

question.text: The PDF describes VETO rights as 'negative control' — the power to oppose a corporate action even when it has the requisite majority. This contrasts with affirmative rights because:

answer.text: Veto rights apply only to listed companies; affirmative rights apply only to unlisted ones
Veto rights and affirmative rights are identical in mechanism
Affirmative rights can be waived; veto rights cannot
Affirmative rights require the investor's prior YES consent for an action to proceed; veto rights allow the investor to say NO to an already-approved action

explanation.text: The Logic: Affirmative = 'YES required' = positive control. Veto = 'NO allowed' = negative control. Both achieve similar protection but framed differently. The PDF explicitly contrasts them: affirmative rights create obligation to seek prior approval; veto rights create defensive power to block. The Trap: They are NOT identical. Listed/unlisted split is fictional. Both can be waived by the rights-holder voluntarily. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tests this distinction. In practice term sheets blend both. Manager's Pro-Tip: Prefer AFFIRMATIVE rights for proactive matters (new capital issue, M&A) because the company MUST come to you. Prefer VETO for reactive, obscure items (related-party transactions) where you can't anticipate every permutation.
